heading: Computer Quiz
intro: Ten questions on the history and basics of computing, across the seven eras of the journey: from bits to paths and memory, all the way to ports and firewalls. After each answer you learn what lies behind it.
scope: A quiz about computer knowledge – not an exam, not an assessment. Your best score stays in this browser only.

byte-bits.question: How many bits make up a byte almost everywhere today?
byte-bits.explanation: Eight bits give 256 patterns of on and off – enough for every letter of the Latin alphabet plus digits and symbols. That is the truth of the 1946 era: text is numbers.

ascii-a.question: Which number stands for the capital letter “A” in ASCII?
ascii-a.explanation: “A” is 65, in binary 01000001; the lowercase “a” is 97. The truth of the 1946 era: to the computer, every character is a number.

three-bits.question: How many different patterns can 3 bits form?
three-bits.explanation: Each bit doubles the possibilities: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8, from 000 to 111. That is how, in the 1946 era, on and off become a whole alphabet.

binary-five.question: Which binary number stands for the decimal number 5?
binary-five.explanation: 101 means 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 5: each digit is worth twice the one to its right. That is the truth of the 1946 era – numbers and text are patterns of bits.

shortest-first.question: Three jobs are waiting for a computer. They take 10, 2 and 5 minutes. In which order is their total waiting time shortest?
shortest-first.explanation: Short jobs first: together they then wait 0 + 2 + 7 = 9 minutes instead of up to 25. The rule is called “shortest job first” – scheduling as in the 1956 era.

first-os.question: What did the first operating systems of the mid-1950s take care of?

options.c: That the computer worked through one job after another without a pause
options.d: Operating the computer with a mouse

first-os.explanation: A mainframe was expensive, and every idle minute between two jobs cost money. The operating system of the 1956 era handled the changeover itself: a computer hates waiting.

batch-meaning.question: What does batch processing mean?

options.a: The computer reacts instantly to every keystroke
options.b: Jobs are collected and worked through one after another without intervention
options.d: Data is backed up to hard disks in batches

batch-meaning.explanation: In the batch operation of the 1956 era, you handed in a deck of punch cards and collected the printout later. Who came next was decided by the order in the batch.

scheduler.question: Which part of an operating system decides which program gets processor time next?
scheduler.explanation: The scheduler shares out processor time – today many times per second, in the 1956 era still job by job.

root.question: What is the topmost directory of a UNIX filesystem called?
root.explanation: Everything hangs from the root “/”, including every additional disk and every USB stick. That is the tree of the 1971 era: every file has a path that starts there.

dot-dot.question: Where does the command “cd ..” take you?

options.d: To the directory you visited last

dot-dot.explanation: In every directory, “..” is the name of the level above. That is how you have climbed up the tree since the 1971 era.

absolute-path.question: Which of these paths is absolute?
absolute-path.explanation: An absolute path starts at the root “/” and works from anywhere; the others depend on where you are standing. A lesson from the 1971 era.

pwd.question: What does the command “pwd” show?

options.d: The path of the current directory

pwd.explanation: pwd stands for “print working directory” and shows where in the tree you are. It is part of the UNIX toolkit from the 1971 era.

conventional-memory.question: How much memory could programs use directly under MS-DOS on the IBM PC?
conventional-memory.explanation: The famous 640 KB of “conventional memory”: the rest of the first megabyte was reserved for the graphics card and the BIOS. The truth of the 1981 era: memory is finite.

kibibyte.question: How many bytes are in a kibibyte (KiB)?
kibibyte.explanation: In the DOS world of the 1981 era, people said “kilobyte” and meant 1024 bytes, 2 to the power of 10. Today that is precisely a kibibyte; an SI kilobyte is 1000 bytes.

ram-power.question: What happens to the contents of memory (RAM) when the power fails?

options.c: They are kept until the next start

ram-power.explanation: RAM holds data only while power flows. That is why people saved to floppy disk in the 1981 era – and why you still save today.

free-memory.question: Under MS-DOS, a program reports: not enough memory. What typically helped?

options.d: Leaving out drivers or loading them into upper memory

free-memory.explanation: Every driver in CONFIG.SYS and AUTOEXEC.BAT took up part of the 640 KB. Anyone who wanted to start a large program in the DOS world of the 1981 era cleared out memory first.

wimp.question: What does the abbreviation WIMP stand for?
wimp.explanation: Windows, icons, menus and a pointer: the four building blocks the Macintosh brought to a wide audience in the 1984 era, and which still shape every interface today.

macintosh-1984.question: What did the Macintosh bring to a wide audience in 1984?

options.b: A graphical interface with a mouse

macintosh-1984.explanation: Graphical interfaces existed before in research labs, for example at Xerox. In the 1984 era, the Macintosh put windows and the mouse on many people's desks.

point-and-choose.question: What is the idea behind a graphical interface?

options.c: Pointing and choosing instead of memorising commands

point-and-choose.explanation: What you can see, you do not have to remember: a menu shows the commands, the mouse picks one. The truth of the 1984 era: pointing is easier than remembering.

copy-shortcut.question: Which key combination copies the selection on a Mac?
copy-shortcut.explanation: C for copy; V pastes, X cuts, Z undoes. In the 1984 era the Macintosh showed these shortcuts right next to the menu commands – whoever saw them often learned them along the way.

ip-address.question: What is an IP address for?

options.d: It identifies a device on the network so packets can find it

ip-address.explanation: No address, no destination: every packet carries the IP addresses of its sender and receiver. The truth of the 1995 era: a network needs addresses.

ipv4-bits.question: How many bits does an IPv4 address have?
ipv4-bits.explanation: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255, such as 192.168.1.20. IPv6 uses 128 bits because IPv4 addresses ran short; in the 1995 era, Windows 95 spoke only IPv4.

gateway.question: What does the default gateway do?

options.a: It forwards packets to destinations outside the local network
options.b: It translates domain names into addresses

gateway.explanation: Everything that is not on the local network goes to the gateway, usually the router. In Windows 95, in the 1995 era, it had its own tab in the TCP/IP settings.

same-network.question: Subnet mask 255.255.255.0: which address is on the same network as 192.168.1.20?
same-network.explanation: This mask says: the first three numbers are the network, the last one is the device. 192.168.1.200 shares the first three with 192.168.1.20 – the arithmetic behind the network puzzle of the 1995 era.

prefix-24.question: Which subnet mask does the notation /24 stand for?
prefix-24.explanation: /24 means the first 24 of the 32 bits are the network: three full groups of eight – 255.255.255.0. Addresses and masks are the truth of the 1995 era.

https-port.question: On which port does a web server accept HTTPS connections by default?
https-port.explanation: 443 for HTTPS, 80 for unencrypted HTTP. A firewall today opens exactly the ports a service needs – and no more.

ssh-port.question: Which service uses port 22 by default?
ssh-port.explanation: Today admins use SSH to manage servers and containers remotely, encrypted. That makes port 22 one of the first a firewall deliberately controls.

port-purpose.question: What are ports for?

options.a: They give a computer's address on the network
options.c: They direct a connection to the right program on a computer

port-purpose.explanation: The IP address finds the computer, the port finds the program on it. Today a single server often runs many services side by side, each behind its own port.

first-match.question: A firewall checks its rules from top to bottom, and the first match applies. Rule 1: block everything. Rule 2: allow port 443. What happens to a connection on port 443?
first-match.explanation: Rule 1 matches everything and applies first; rule 2 never gets its turn. The allow rule has to sit above the block – the principle behind today's firewall puzzle.

container.question: What is a container, for example with Docker?

options.a: A physical server in a data centre
options.c: Another word for a hard disk
options.d: A program with everything it needs, isolated from others on the same system

container.explanation: A container brings its program along with its libraries and runs sealed off, on a laptop just as in the cloud. The truth of today: programs run isolated, in many places at once.
